ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: In the image, a horizontal conducting rod is labeled AB, with the left end as A and the right end as B; point C is located at a position slightly to the right on the rod. The dashed axis OO' passes vertically through C and is perpendicular to rod AB. The figure also draws an arrow for magnetic induction intensity B, whose direction is the same as axis OO'; the angular velocity ω is also marked near this axis, indicating that the conducting rod rotates around the axis passing through C. According to the problem statement and the figure, take C as the origin, and take the x-axis along the conducting rod from left to right; the coordinate of the right-side B end is x=+BC, and the coordinate of the left-side A end is x=-AC. The magnetic field direction is parallel to the angular velocity direction. For a point on the rod, the velocity is v=ω×r, so the component of v×B in the direction of the rod is proportional to x: when x>0, it points in the +x direction, and when x<0, it points in the -x direction. When the conductor reaches electrostatic equilibrium, the internal electric field satisfies E=−v×B. Also because E_x=−dV/dx, dV/dx is proportional to x, and integration gives V(x)−V(C)=1/2·Bωx^2. The problem gives BC=1/3 AB, therefore AC=2/3 AB. The distance from point A to C is greater than the distance from point B to C, so V_A−V_C is greater than V_B−V_C. Therefore V_A>V_B.

method.method_draft: Set the origin at C and take the rod as the x-axis, with B-end at x=+BC and A-end at x=-AC. From the image/text, the magnetic field and angular velocity are parallel along OO'. For a point at coordinate x on the rod, v = ω × r, so v × B points in the +x direction when x>0 and in the -x direction when x<0; in compact form it is proportional to x along the rod. In electrostatic equilibrium inside the rod, E = -v × B, so dV/dx is proportional to x. Integrate to get V(x)-V(C) = (1/2)Bωx^2. Since BC=L/3 and AC=2L/3, point A is farther from C than point B, so V_A - V_C is larger than V_B - V_C. Therefore V_A > V_B.

method.method_draft: Treat CA and CB as two rotating conducting spokes sharing the same axis point C. Because ω is parallel to B, the magnetic force on positive charges in each half of the rod is radially outward from C, so both outer ends are at higher potential than C. Apply the rotating-rod potential formula: the potential elevation of an end relative to C is proportional to the square of its distance from C. The text gives BC=L/3, so AC=2L/3. ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
In the image, a horizontal conducting rod is labeled AB, with the left end as A and the right end as B; point C is located at a position slightly to the right on the rod. The dashed axis OO' passes vertically through C and is perpendicular to rod AB. The figure also draws an arrow for magnetic induction intensity B, whose direction is the same as axis OO'; the angular velocity ω is also marked near this axis, indicating that the conducting rod rotates around the axis passing through C.

According to the problem statement and the figure, take C as the origin, and take the x-axis along the conducting rod from left to right; the coordinate of the right-side B end is x=+BC, and the coordinate of the left-side A end is x=-AC. The magnetic field direction is parallel to the angular velocity direction. For a point on the rod, the velocity is v=ω×r, so the component of v×B in the direction of the rod is proportional to x: when x>0, it points in the +x direction, and when x<0, it points in the -x direction. When the conductor reaches electrostatic equilibrium, the internal electric field satisfies E=−v×B. Also because E_x=−dV/dx, dV/dx is proportional to x, and integration gives V(x)−V(C)=1/2·Bωx^2. The problem gives BC=1/3 AB, therefore AC=2/3 AB. The distance from point A to C is greater than the distance from point B to C, so V_A−V_C is greater than V_B−V_C. Therefore V_A>V_B.
